results.claim: Complement equivalence and exact endpoint cases. Let F(n,k) count labelled graphs on [n] with vertex-cover number at most k, let N=binom(n,2), and put m=n−k. For 0≤k≤n, F(n,k)=2^N−T(n,m), where T(n,m) is the number of labelled K_m-free graphs. Consequently F(n,n−3)=2^N−T(n,3), with T(n,3) the triangle-free graph count. Also F(n,0)=1; F(n,1)=1+n(2^{n−1}−1)−binom(n,2); F(n,n−2)=2^N−1; and F(n,n−1)=F(n,n)=2^N.
results.proof_sketch: For every graph G, a set C is a vertex cover exactly when V(G)\C is independent. Hence τ(G)=n−α(G), and τ(G)≤k exactly when G has an independent m-set. Complementation turns independent m-sets into K_m subgraphs, proving the identity. For k=1, every admissible edge set is a subset of one of the n labelled stars. The empty graph is counted once; a one-edge graph is counted twice in the star sum; and any admissible graph with at least two edges has a unique common center. This gives the displayed formula. The remaining endpoint formulas follow immediately from requiring independent sets of sizes two or one.

results.claim: Two-sided family-size lower bounds. For 2≤m≤n, put r=m−1, write n=ar+s with 0≤s<r, and let e(n,m)=[n²−s(a+1)²−(r−s)a²]/2. Then T(n,m)≥2^{e(n,m)} and F(n,n−m)≥2^{N−binom(m,2)}. For fixed m≥3, e(n,m)=(m−2)n²/[2(m−1)]+O_m(1); specifically e(n,3)=floor(n²/4).
results.proof_sketch: Fix a balanced partition of [n] into r=m−1 labelled parts: s have size a+1 and r−s have size a. There are exactly e(n,m) cross-part pairs. Every arbitrary subset of these pairs defines a distinct r-partite graph, which cannot contain K_{r+1}=K_m by the pigeonhole principle. This gives the lower bound on T. For the other bound, fix one particular m-set S and require its binom(m,2) internal pairs to be absent. Every subset of the remaining N−binom(m,2) pairs gives a distinct graph in which S is independent, hence counted by F(n,n−m). The displayed asymptotic follows by substituting n=ar+s; for r=2 the cross-pair count is floor(n²/4).

results.claim: Enumeration-strategy obstruction and its sharp endpoint boundary. For every fixed m≥3, both F(n,n−m) and T(n,m) have 2^{Θ(n²)} members. More generally, if m≥3 and k=n−m≥cn for a constant c>0, both families have 2^{Ω(n²)} members. Thus an algorithm that explicitly lists every admissible graph, or instead every K_m-free graph before subtracting from 2^N, cannot run in 2^{o(n²)} time in this regime. At m=2, T(n,2)=1, whereas at m=3 already T(n,3)≥2^{floor(n²/4)}; hence k=n−3 is the first fixed-distance-from-n endpoint where neither side can be explicitly enumerated within the target time. This does not prove a lower bound against implicit exact counting.
results.proof_sketch: The preceding bounds and the trivial upper bound 2^N prove the fixed-m statement. For the more general regime, q=N−binom(m,2)=kn−k(k+1)/2=k(2n−k−1)/2≥k(n−1)/2=Ω(n²), so F≥2^q. For every m≥3, all subgraphs of one fixed balanced complete bipartite graph are K_m-free, giving T≥2^{floor(n²/4)}. Explicitly listing a family requires at least one listing step per member. In contrast, a K_2-free graph has no edges, so T(n,2)=1. A uniform target algorithm at k=n−3 would yield T(n,3)=2^N−F(n,n−3) by one subtraction, but these cardinality bounds only force such an algorithm to aggregate implicitly; they do not constrain all possible counting methods.

results.claim: There is a deterministic exact algorithm using polynomial space and time 2^{q+O(n)}, where q=binom(n,2)−binom(n−k,2)=kn−k(k+1)/2. Therefore the target is achieved whenever k=o(n), including k=O(n/log n).
results.proof_sketch: For every k-subset C⊆[n], generate the 2^q graphs having no edge inside [n]\C. For each generated graph, inspect all k-subsets preceding C in a fixed lexicographic order and count the graph only if none is a vertex cover. Every graph with τ≤k has a k-element cover, obtained by extending any smaller cover, and it is generated and retained exactly for its first k-cover. There are binom(n,k)2^q generated pairs, and the canonicality test uses at most binom(n,k) polynomial-time cover tests. Thus the time is poly(n)·binom(n,k)^2·2^q=2^{q+O(n)}, with only the current graph and counters stored. If k=o(n), then q≤nk=o(n²).

results.claim: Structural hard-strip reduction. For n≥2 let ℓ(n)=floor(n/ceil(log₂n)). A deterministic exact 2^{o(n²)}-time algorithm for every 0≤k≤n exists if and only if one exists uniformly on the restricted strip ℓ(n)<k≤n−3. Equivalently, under m=n−k, the only unresolved range needed for the full target is 3≤m≤n−ℓ(n)−1.
results.proof_sketch: The forward implication follows by restricting any uniform target algorithm. Conversely, suppose an exact algorithm with uniform running time 2^{o(n²)} is available on the displayed strip. If k≤ℓ(n), use the preceding canonical-cover algorithm: q≤nk≤n²/ceil(log₂n), so q+O(n)=o(n²). If k≥n−2, use the exact endpoint formulas, which require only polynomial-time integer arithmetic. Every integer k not covered by those two cases satisfies ℓ(n)<k≤n−3 and is handled by the assumed restricted algorithm. The case n=1 is immediate. Thus the three branches form a uniform exact 2^{o(n²)} algorithm. Finally, k>ℓ(n) is equivalent, for integral m=n−k, to m≤n−ℓ(n)−1, while k≤n−3 is equivalent to m≥3.

results.claim: For every fixed k there is a polynomial-time exact algorithm. More explicitly, F(n,k) is computable in time at most poly(n)·sum_{t=0}^k binom(n,t)·2^{binom(t,2)+t}·[2(t+2)]^{2^t−1}.
results.proof_sketch: Count graphs of vertex-cover number exactly t by their lexicographically first minimum cover C. Fix C and H=G[C]. Write I=[n]\C; I must be independent, and each v∈I is described by its neighborhood type A_v⊆C. For every nonempty independent X⊆V(H), let U_X={v∈I:A_v∩X≠∅}. Replacing X in C by U_X gives a cover, so C is minimum exactly when |U_X|≥|X| for every such X. When equality holds, this is another minimum cover; C precedes it exactly when min X<min U_X. Scan I in label order. For each X, a dynamic-programming state stores |U_X| capped at |X|+1 and whether U_X contains a label below min X. Choosing one of 2^t neighborhood types updates every coordinate. The final conditions are |U_X|>|X|, or equality without a below-minimum label. There are at most 2^t−1 coordinates and at most 2(t+2) values per coordinate. Summing over C and the 2^{binom(t,2)} choices of H yields the bound and counts every graph exactly once.

results.claim: Exact first- and second-moment formulas give certified bounds for all parameters. For 1≤m≤n, let q=N−binom(m,2), S1=binom(n,m)2^q, and S2=binom(n,m)·sum_{j=max(0,2m−n)}^m binom(m,j)binom(n−m,m−j)2^{N−2binom(m,2)+binom(j,2)}. Then max{2^q, ceil(S1²/S2)}≤F(n,n−m)≤min{2^N,S1}. In particular, q≤log₂F(n,n−m)≤q+n.
results.proof_sketch: For a graph G let X(G) be its number of independent m-subsets. Summing over a chosen m-set gives sum_G X(G)=S1. For an ordered pair S,T with |S∩T|=j, independence of both forces exactly 2binom(m,2)−binom(j,2) edges to be absent. Counting such ordered pairs gives S2=sum_G X(G)^2. The upper bound follows from 1_{X>0}≤X. Cauchy–Schwarz gives S1²≤F·S2. Finally, fixing one particular independent m-set supplies 2^q distinct qualifying graphs. The logarithmic bracket uses binom(n,m)≤2^n.

results.claim: At the triangle-free endpoint, a substantial subclass is exactly countable in polynomial time. Let B_n be the number of labelled bipartite graphs and P_n=sum_{a=0}^n binom(n,a)2^{a(n−a)}. Then B_0=1 and B_n=(P_n−sum_{a=1}^{n−1}binom(n,a)B_aB_{n−a})/2. Hence F(n,n−3)≤2^N−B_n is an exact-arithmetic, polynomial-time computable bound.
results.proof_sketch: P_n counts pairs consisting of a bipartite graph and an ordered proper two-coloring: choose the first color class and then choose arbitrary cross edges. If C(x) is the exponential generating series for connected bipartite graphs, then uncolored bipartite graphs have series B(x)=exp(C(x)). Every connected bipartite graph has exactly two ordered proper two-colorings, including an isolated vertex, so the colored series is P(x)=exp(2C(x))=B(x)^2. Comparing degree-n coefficients yields the recurrence. Every bipartite graph is triangle-free, so B_n≤T(n,3), and the complement identity gives the stated bound.

results.claim: Direct distinguished-vertex recurrence for the triangle-free endpoint. Let 𝒯_r be the set of labelled triangle-free graphs on [r], and let i(H) include the empty set in the number of independent vertex sets of H. Then T(0,3)=1 and, for n≥1, T(n,3)=sum_{d=0}^{n−1} binom(n−1,d)·sum_{H∈𝒯_{n−1−d}} i(H)^d. Equivalently, T(n,3)=nT(n−1,3)+sum_{d=2}^{n−1} binom(n−1,d)·sum_{H∈𝒯_{n−1−d}} i(H)^d.
results.proof_sketch: Fix a distinguished vertex v, choose its d-element neighborhood S, and put R=V\(S∪{v}). Triangle-freeness forces S to be independent. After choosing H=G[R]∈𝒯_{n−1−d}, each s∈S independently chooses an independent vertex set of H as its neighborhood in R, giving i(H)^d choices. Conversely these data create no triangle: one inside R is excluded by H, one using v or two vertices of S is excluded because S is independent, and one using exactly one s∈S and two vertices of R is excluded by the chosen independent neighborhood. The construction is reversible and there are binom(n−1,d) choices for S, proving the first recurrence. The d=0 and d=1 contributions are respectively T(n−1,3) and (n−1)T(n−1,3), proving the second.

results.claim: The distinguished-vertex recurrence gives a deterministic exact algorithm for F(n,n−3) in time poly(n)·2^{binom(n−3,2)} with exponential space, or time poly(n)·2^{binom(n−2,2)} with polynomial space, for n≥3. Both exponents remain Θ(n²), so neither algorithm achieves the requested 2^{o(n²)} strength.
results.proof_sketch: By the complement identity it suffices to evaluate T(n,3). After replacing the d=0,1 terms by nT(n−1,3), every new moment uses r=n−1−d≤n−3 vertices. All i(H) on r vertices can be tabulated in poly(r)·2^{binom(r,2)} time: initialize a[K(A)] by counting vertex sets A with clique-edge set K(A), take the subset-zeta transform g(E)=sum_{D⊆E}a[D], and use i(H)=g[binom([r],2)\E(H)]. Enumerating H, testing triangle-freeness, and summing i(H)^d then gives the exponential-space bound, dominated by r=n−3. Alternatively compute i(H) by checking all 2^r subsets separately for each H. This uses polynomial space, and binom(r,2)+r is maximized at binom(n−2,2). Recursive smaller orders are dominated, and all accumulators have O(n²) bits. Finally both displayed binomial exponents divided by n² tend to 1/2.

final_writeup:
The full uniform target remains unresolved. Writing m=n−k reduces the problem to exact counting of K_m-free graphs. The obstruction attempt establishes a precise limitation of direct enumeration: fixing an independent m-set gives at least 2^{N−binom(m,2)} admissible graphs, while a fixed balanced (m−1)-partition gives at least 2^{e(n,m)} K_m-free graphs. Consequently, for fixed m≥3—and more generally when k is bounded below by a positive linear fraction of n and m≥3—both sides contain 2^{Ω(n²)} graphs. An algorithm meeting the target must aggregate implicitly rather than enumerate either family. This boundary is sharp for that strategy: T(n,2)=1, but T(n,3)≥2^{floor(n²/4)}. These cardinality bounds are not a lower bound against arbitrary exact counting, so they do not solve the open target.

The structural-reduction lens isolates the remaining parameter range exactly. Put ℓ(n)=floor(n/ceil(log₂n)) for n≥2. The uniform target is equivalent to constructing the requested algorithm only for ℓ(n)<k≤n−3, or equivalently 3≤m≤n−ℓ(n)−1. Below this strip, the canonical-cover algorithm has exponent at most n²/ceil(log₂n)+O(n)=o(n²); above it, the exact endpoint formulas apply. The reverse transfer simply dispatches among these cases. This reduction still contains k=n−3 for all sufficiently large n, so it does not bypass the triangle-free endpoint or change the target-coverage verdict.

The canonical-cover algorithm runs in time 2^{kn−k(k+1)/2+O(n)} and achieves 2^{o(n²)} whenever k=o(n), including k=O(n/log n). The fixed-k dynamic program is polynomial for each fixed k, but its parameter dependence does not handle growing linear k. At k=n−3, the distinguished-vertex recurrence computes the exact triangle-free count, and hence F(n,n−3), in time poly(n)·2^{binom(n−3,2)} with exponential space or poly(n)·2^{binom(n−2,2)} with polynomial space. Both remain 2^{Θ(n²)}. The moment identities give certified general bounds, and the bipartite recurrence gives a polynomial-time endpoint bound, not an exact uniform algorithm. The claimed resolution therefore remains PARTIAL, matching the audit’s target-coverage judgment.
